title: Work Extraction via Backward Motion in Optimal Closed-Loop Stochastic Control
authors: Luis Frieder Reinalter, Emanuele Panizon, Lokesh Muruga, Clemens Bechinger
abstract: We experimentally realize finite-time feedback control in an overdamped colloidal system using real-time optical tweezers with in situ reinforcement learning (RL). By varying the protocol duration tf for displacing the optical trap between prescribed positions, the optimal strategies identified by RL reveal a crossover from deterministic dragging toward the target to feedback-assisted exploitation of thermal fluctuations, reducing and eventually overcoming the energetic cost. The resulting policies agree quantitatively with the exact optimal closed-loop solution. By extending the approach to spatially localized external forcing, we further show that RL can identify optimal feedback strategies in heterogeneous stochastic environments where direct analytical control design is challenging.
summary: The authors experimentally demonstrate using reinforcement learning (RL) that feedback control can extract usable work from thermal baths in colloidal systems. They show this occurs via specific 'backward' trap movements, which is confirmed by comparing RL results against exact theoretical solutions derived from stochastic control theory. The methodology is robust enough to handle complex, externally forced environments.
main_problem: The research investigates how optimal closed-loop feedback control can minimize energetic costs when steering a physical system toward a target state in the presence of thermal fluctuations.
main_result: Optimal policies identified via Reinforcement Learning (RL) quantitatively match analytical solutions, demonstrating that work extraction ($\langle W angle < 0$) occurs by exploiting backward trap displacements, even extending to heterogeneous non-equilibrium environments.
method: The study combines experimental realization using real-time optical tweezers and in situ RL (PPO) with rigorous theoretical analysis derived from stochastic control theory (LQG formulation).
model_or_system: The system is an overdamped colloidal particle suspended in a water–glycerol mixture, controlled by time-varying optical traps. The dynamics are governed by stochastic processes influenced by thermal noise.
key_observables: Average work ($\langle W angle$) as a function of protocol duration ($t_f$), and the classification of feedback actions into quadrants based on trap displacement ($\Delta\lambda$) versus work increment ($\Delta W$).
important_parameters: Trap stiffness ($\kappa = 2 \pm 0.2 	ext{ pN}/\mu	ext{m}$), viscous relaxation time ($	au_r \approx 25 	ext{ ms}$), and the protocol duration ($t_f$) which dictates the crossover regime.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that RL can successfully learn optimal policies without requiring a detailed dynamical model, although theoretical benchmarks are used for comparison.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate $\langle W angle$ vs $t_f$, showing work extraction at long times; action distributions classify feedback into quadrants (Q1-Q4); and later figures map out these quadrant probabilities in both equilibrium and non-equilibrium settings.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the experimental setup and RL methodology for optimal control. It then analyzes the crossover of work cost with protocol time, identifying backward motion as key to energy extraction. Finally, it extends this analysis to heterogeneous external forcing fields, confirming the robustness of the feedback strategy.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful demonstration of how machine learning can solve complex optimal control problems in physical systems, offering insights into non-equilibrium thermodynamics and fluctuation-driven energy harvesting that are highly relevant to open quantum systems research.

Symbols are experimental values obtained from RL-identified optimal policies, the solid and dashed lines denotes the ana- lytical solution for the optimal closed-loop protocol and that without feedback. Insets: representative trap trajectories λt and corresponding particle trajectories xt for tf = 0.2 s and 3 s. For tf = 0.2 s, the particle systematically lags behind the trap, and variations between experiments are barely visible. For tf = 3 s, the particle remains closer to the trap trajectory, and individual realizations exhibit much larger scatter (gray band denotes scatter across 100 repeated realizations).

Figure 2. (a)–(c) Representative action distributions for tf = 0.5 s, 1 s, and 3 s, respectively, classified by trap displacement ∆λ and work increment ∆W. Forward and backward steps correspond to positive and negative ∆λ, respectively. The quadrants denote forward work-costing steps (Q1), backward work-costing steps (Q2), backward work-extracting steps (Q3), and forward work-extracting steps (Q4). Short protocols are dominated by Q1, whereas increasing tf enhances the population of work- extracting Q3 events. (d) Normalized quadrant occupation probabilities P(Qi) as a function of tf. The blue curve shows a single realization of the optimal feedback protocol identified by RL, while the gray band indicates the scatter between 100 individual experiments. The trap trajectory first approaches the perturbed region, remains there for an extended part of the protocol, and then reaches the target. Figure 4. Schematic of the experimental optical-tweezer setup. A silica colloid is confined in an optical trap generated by a focused trapping laser. The trap position is controlled by a piezo-actuated steering mirror, while the particle position is recorded by video microscopy. The measured particle posi- tion, current trap position, and protocol time are passed to a real-time controller, which computes the next trap displace- ment. External perturbations can be applied by translating the sample with a piezo stage.
